case_title: Ramesh Harijan v. State of U.P.
accused_victim_relationship: Neighbour (the accused's house was adjacent to the house where the victim's grandmother lived); no other relationship stated
evidence_type: Eyewitness (PW.7, PW.8 saw the rape; PW.1 last seen and alleged extra-judicial confession); medical (post-mortem and serology); recovery (bed sheet and cloth with blood and semen); circumstantial (last seen together)
confession: Alleged extra-judicial confession (PW.1 testified to it). Trial court disbelieved it as not made in the presence of PW.7 and PW.8; the Supreme Court did not rely on it
aggravating_circumstances: Victim a child aged 5-6 years; rape with vaginal injuries leading to death; victim had been left in the accused's neighbourhood
trial_court_outcome: Acquitted of both charges (s.302 and s.376 IPC); no sentence
high_court_outcome: State appeal allowed; acquittal reversed; convicted under ss.302 and 376 IPC; life imprisonment on both counts, sentences concurrent
neutral_facts: A girl aged about five to six years was found dead on a cot in a village where she was staying with her blind, infirm maternal grandmother, who was too poor and unable to care for her. The girl's grandmother's thatched house had collapsed, so the grandmother and the girl used to sleep in a house very close by, which belonged to the accused. The victim's mother was first told the girl had died of paralysis, and the body was buried on a riverbank. Later, the mother received information from several villagers that the girl had been raped and killed by the accused, and she asked for the body to be exhumed. After an order of the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, the body was dug out and examined on 3.2.1996 by two doctors. They found multiple contusions on the face, neck, shoulder and back, and vaginal injuries including lacerations, and stated that the death was caused by shock and haemorrhage from ante-mortem vaginal injuries. One witness deposed that he had been returning home at about 9.00 p.m. with a companion, heard whispering near the accused's house, and focused a torch and saw the accused raping the girl beneath a tree outside the house. The companion raised a cry, villagers gathered, and the accused ran away. Another witness deposed that the accused had confessed the crime to him in the presence of two others. A part of a bed sheet and white cloth were recovered during the investigation, and forensic examination found human blood and semen on them, as well as on a vaginal swab taken by the doctor. The accused was arrested at a road junction in the early hours of the following day while waiting for transport. Several other witnesses did not support the prosecution account.
physical_harm: Death of the child from shock and haemorrhage due to ante-mortem vaginal injuries; multiple contusions and abrasions on face, neck, shoulder and back; vaginal tears and lacerations
key_evidence_accepted: Recovery of bed sheet and white cloth with blood and semen (serology report, vaginal swab); medical evidence of ante-mortem vaginal injuries; last seen evidence of PW.1, PW.7 and PW.8 accepted at least that the deceased was last seen with the accused; hostile witnesses' relevant parts usable
witness_credibility: Court accepted some exaggeration in PW.1, PW.7 and PW.8 but held minor discrepancies unimportant and the duty of the court is to unravel truth; hostile witnesses' evidence not discarded as a whole; PW.1's alleged enmity rejected as unproven on the time gap; trial court's reliance on discrepancies held erroneous
post_offence_conduct: Ran out when villagers gathered after the witness's cry (per PW.7); arrested at 3.35 a.m. at a road junction while waiting for transport
trial_duration: offence: 30.1.1996; trial judgment: 2.2.1999; High Court: 23.3.2007; Supreme Court: 21.05.2012
legal_representation: Accused: Rajender Pd. Saxena. State: Vikrant Yadav, Jyoti Sharma, Vinay Kumar Garg, Gunnam Venkateswara Rao (for the respondent)
investigation_status: FIR lodged 2.2.1996 at Haraiya Police Station; Case Crime No. 22 of 1996 registered; investigation completed; chargesheet filed; trial completed with 14 prosecution witnesses
procedural_irregularity: None noted (trial court's adverse inference for non-examination of the grandmother and failure to consider depositions were errors in appreciation, not procedural lapses)
appeal_history: Trial court: acquitted of both charges. High Court: State appeal allowed, convicted on both counts. Supreme Court: accused's appeal dismissed
prosecution_argument: The High Court reversal was correct; the findings were based on correct appreciation of evidence and no interference was warranted
defence_argument: Witnesses PW.1, PW.7 and PW.8 were motivated and their improvements meant their evidence should be discarded; other witnesses turned hostile; no evidence the child slept at the accused's house; High Court findings perverse
legal_principle_applied: Appellate interference with acquittal only in exceptional cases where the acquittal is perverse; hostile witness evidence cannot be discarded as a whole; falsus in uno maxim not applicable in India; reasonable doubt must be fair, not fanciful
precedent_relied_upon: State of Rajasthan v. Talevar (AIR 2011 SC 2271); State of U.P. v. Mohd. Iqram (AIR 2011 SC 2296); Govindaraju v. State (2012) 4 SCC 722; State of Haryana v. case_title.quote: RAMESH HARIJAN v. STATE OF U.P. (Criminal Appeal No. 1340 of 2007)

number_of_accused.quote: The appellant-accused was prosecuted for having raped and caused death of minor girl aged 5-6 years.

victim_gender.quote: her daughter Renu, aged 5-6 years, was found dead on her cot in Muradipur

victim_age.quote: Renu, aged 5-6 years of age, died of vaginal injuries.

statutory_provisions.quote: the High Court has convicted the appellant for the offence punishable under Sections 302 and 376 of Indian Penal Code, 1860

evidence_type.quote: The prosecution has examined Kunwar Dhruv Narain Singh (PW.1), the scribe of the FIR

confession.quote: Such statement had not been made by either of the said witnesses.

aggravating_circumstances.quote: Renu, aged 5-6 years of age, died of vaginal injuries.

trial_court_outcome.quote: the trial court vide its judgment and order dated 2.2.1999 acquitted the appellant of both the aforesaid charges.

high_court_outcome.quote: The appeal preferred by the State was allowed by High Court, convicting the accused for both the charges.

final_outcome.quote: the appeal lacks, merit and is accordingly dismissed.

offence_finally_established.quote: the High Court has convicted the appellant for the offence punishable under Sections 302 and 376 of Indian Penal Code, 1860

imprisonment_type.quote: awarded him the life imprisonment for both the offences. However, both the sentences have been directed to run concurrently.

neutral_facts.quote: Renu, aged 5-6 years, was found dead on her cot in Muradipur, the village of her maternal grandmother on 30.1.1996 at about 9.00 p.m.

attempt_completion.quote: Renu, aged 5-6 years of age, died of vaginal injuries.

physical_harm.quote: In their opinion, death was due to shock and haemorrhage as a result of ante-mortem vaginal injuries.

number_of_offences.quote: the High Court has convicted the appellant for the offence punishable under Sections 302 and 376

key_evidence_accepted.quote: The recovery of part of the sheet and white clothes having blood and semen as per the FSL report has been dis-believed by the trial court

witness_credibility.quote: Undoubtedly, there may be some exaggeration in the evidence of the prosecution witnesses, particularly, that of Kunwar Dhruv Narain Singh (PW.1 ), Jata Shankar Singh (PW.7) and Shitla Prasad Verma (PW.8).

post_offence_conduct.quote: the appellant Ramesh ran out. The girl had died of rape.

trial_duration.quote: the trial court vide its judgment and order dated 2.2.1999 acquitted the appellant

legal_representation.quote: Rajender Pd. Saxena for the Appellant. Vikrant Yadav, Jyoti Sharma, Vinay Kumar Garg, Gunnam Venkateswara Rao for the Respondent.

investigation_status.quote: Case Crime No. 22 of 1996 was registered against the appellant under Sections 302 and 376 IPC. After having the investigation, the police filed the chargesheet against the appellant.

procedural_irregularity.quote: The trial court ought not to have drawn adverse inference for not examining Smt. Phulpatta Devi by the prosecution.

appeal_history.quote: The appeal preferred by the State was allowed by High Court, convicting the accused for both the charges. Hence, the present appeal by the accused.

prosecution_argument.quote: the judgment of the trial court has rightly been reversed by the High Court being contrary to the evidence on record. The High Court has recorded the findings of fact on correct appreciation of evidence.

defence_argument.quote: The evidence relied upon by the High Court particularly that of Kunwar Dhruv Narain Singh (PW.1), Jata Shankar Singh (PW.7) and Shitla Prasad Verma (PW.8) cannot stand judicial scrutiny as these witnesses had been motivated

legal_principle_applied.quote: only in exceptional cases where there are compelling circumstances and the judgment in appeal is found to be perverse, the appellate court can interfere with the order of the acquittal.

precedent_relied_upon.quote: State of Rajasthan v. Talevar and Anr. AIR 2011 SC 2271; State of UP. v. Mohd. Iqram and Anr. AIR 2011 SC 2296
